exam: A 9‑month‑old boy has a unilateral non‑palpable testis. What is the next step? — Perform a careful inguinal examination; if still non‑palpable, arrange ultrasound or refer for diagnostic laparoscopy.

How does a retractile testis differ from cryptorchidism on exam? — Retractile testis can be brought down into the scrotum and stays there with gentle traction; cryptorchid testis cannot be fully descended.
Which complication of an undescended testis is most likely to present in the first year of life? — Inguinal hernia causing obstruction or incarceration.

Why is hormonal therapy (hCG) rarely recommended in low‑resource settings? — Limited efficacy, need for repeated injections, and risk of side‑effects; surgical orchiopexy is more reliable and cost‑effective.
A 2‑year‑old with an abdominal testis is scheduled for surgery. What additional procedure should be performed? — Herniotomy if an associated inguinal hernia is present.
What long‑term surveillance is required after successful orchiopexy? — Annual scrotal examination after puberty, patient education on self‑exam, and ultrasound if any mass is felt.

Explain why testicular cancer risk remains elevated even after orchiopexy. — Pre‑malignant intratubular germ cell neoplasia may have already developed before surgery; orchiopexy reduces but does not eliminate risk.
In a setting without ultrasound, how would you locate a non‑palpable testis? — Proceed to diagnostic laparoscopy, which both confirms location and allows immediate orchiopexy.
ai.title: Undescended Testis (Cryptorchidism)
ai.subject: Paediatrics
ai.summary: Undescended testis is a common congenital condition where the testis fails to descend into the scrotum. Early recognition and timely orchiopexy reduce infertility and cancer risk, especially in low‑resource settings.

b: Palpable testis in inguinal canal = true cryptorchidism
Non‑palpable testis = may be intra‑abdominal or absent
sections.p: A testis that is not palpable within the scrotal sac by 6 months of age (or by 12 months if born preterm) is classified as undescended. Diagnosis is clinical, based on palpation of the inguinal canal, abdomen, or thigh.

b: Canalicular (inguinal) – most common, easier to access surgically
Abdominal – higher malignancy risk, may need laparoscopy
Ectopic (e.g., femoral, perineal) – rare, requires specific approach

Genetic syndromes – e.g., Klinefelter, Prader‑Willi
Intra‑uterine infections – HIV, malaria, syphilis
Local factors – inguinal hernia, hydrocele, testicular torsion in utero
sections.p: Most cases are idiopathic, but several factors increase risk, especially in tropical, low‑resource settings.
